claim: Epistasis determines how a genotype maps onto a phenotype.
source: The interaction between individual mutations – epistasis – determines how a genotype maps onto a phenotype (Wolf et al., 2000; Phillips, 2008; Breen et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Wolf et al., 2000; Phillips, 2008; and Breen et al., 2012.

claim: Epistasis determines the structure of the fitness landscape.
source: As such, it determines the structure of the fitness landscape (de Visser and Krug, 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to de Visser and Krug, 2014.

claim: Epistasis plays a crucial role in defining adaptive pathways and evolutionary outcomes of complex genetic systems.
source: it determines the structure of the fitness landscape (de Visser and Krug, 2014) and plays a crucial role in defining adaptive pathways and evolutionary outcomes of complex genetic systems (Sackton and Hartl, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sackton and Hartl, 2016.

claim: Epistasis influences the repeatability of evolution.
source: For example, epistasis influences the repeatability of evolution (Weinreich et al., 2006; Woods et al., 2011; Szendro et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Weinreich et al., 2006; Woods et al., 2011; and Szendro et al., 2013.

claim: Epistasis influences the benefits of sexual reproduction.
source: epistasis influences the repeatability of evolution (Weinreich et al., 2006; Woods et al., 2011; Szendro et al., 2013), the benefits of sexual reproduction (Kondrashov, 1988)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kondrashov, 1988.

claim: Epistasis influences species divergence.
source: the benefits of sexual reproduction (Kondrashov, 1988), and species divergence (Orr and Turelli, 2001; Dettman et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Orr and Turelli, 2001 and Dettman et al., 2007.

claim: Studies of epistasis have been limited to empirical statistical descriptions.
source: Studies of epistasis have been limited to empirical statistical descriptions, and mostly focused on interactions between individual mutations in structural proteins and enzymes (Phillips, 2008; Starr and Thornton, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Phillips, 2008 and Starr and Thornton, 2016.

claim: Studies of epistasis have mostly focused on interactions between individual mutations in structural proteins and enzymes.
source: Studies of epistasis have been limited to empirical statistical descriptions, and mostly focused on interactions between individual mutations in structural proteins and enzymes (Phillips, 2008; Starr and Thornton, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Phillips, 2008 and Starr and Thornton, 2016.

claim: Studies of epistasis have identified a wide range of possible interactions.
source: While identifying a wide range of possible interactions (Figure 1), these studies have not led to a consensus on whether there is a systematic bias on the sign of epistasis (Lalić and Elena, 2013; Kussell, 2013; Velenich and Gore, 2013; Kondrashov and Kondrashov, 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by a reference to Figure 1 and citations to multiple studies.

claim: Studies of epistasis have not led to a consensus on whether there is a systematic bias on the sign of epistasis.
source: these studies have not led to a consensus on whether there is a systematic bias on the sign of epistasis (Lalić and Elena, 2013; Kussell, 2013; Velenich and Gore, 2013; Kondrashov and Kondrashov, 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lalić and Elena, 2013; Kussell, 2013; Velenich and Gore, 2013; and Kondrashov and Kondrashov, 2015.

claim: The sign of epistasis is a critical feature determining the ruggedness of the fitness landscape.
source: whether there is a systematic bias on the sign of epistasis (Lalić and Elena, 2013; Kussell, 2013; Velenich and Gore, 2013; Kondrashov and Kondrashov, 2015), a critical feature determining the ruggedness of the fitness landscape (Poelwijk et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Poelwijk et al., 2011.

claim: Sign epistasis allows the fitness landscape to have multiple fitness peaks.
source: Specifically, it is only when mutations are in sign epistasis that the fitness landscape can have multiple fitness peaks - a feature that determines the number of evolutionary paths that are accessible to Darwinian adaptation (de Visser and Krug, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to de Visser and Krug, 2014.

claim: Sign epistasis determines the number of evolutionary paths that are accessible to Darwinian adaptation.
source: it is only when mutations are in sign epistasis that the fitness landscape can have multiple fitness peaks - a feature that determines the number of evolutionary paths that are accessible to Darwinian adaptation (de Visser and Krug, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to de Visser and Krug, 2014.

claim: A pattern of positive or negative epistasis has consequences for the maintenance of genetic diversity.
source: Furthermore, even a pattern of positive or negative epistasis has consequences for important evolutionary questions such as the maintenance of genetic diversity (Charlesworth et al., 1995)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Charlesworth et al., 1995.

claim: A pattern of positive or negative epistasis has consequences for the evolution of sex.
source: even a pattern of positive or negative epistasis has consequences for important evolutionary questions such as the maintenance of genetic diversity (Charlesworth et al., 1995) and the evolution of sex (Kondrashov, 1988; Otto and Lenormand, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kondrashov, 1988 and Otto and Lenormand, 2002.

claim: The inability to predict protein structure from sequence prevents the development of a predictive theory of epistasis.
source: The inability to predict structure from sequence, due to the prohibitively large sequence space that would need to be experimentally explored in order to understand even just the effects of point mutations (Maerkl and Quake, 2009; Shultzaberger et al., 2012), let alone the interactions between them, prevents the development of a predictive theory of epistasis (Lehner, 2013; de Visser and Krug, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Maerkl and Quake, 2009; Shultzaberger et al., 2012; Lehner, 2013; and de Visser and Krug, 2014.

claim: The only predictive models of epistasis focus on tractable systems where it is possible to connect the effects of mutations to the underlying biophysical and molecular mechanisms.
source: In fact, the only predictive models of epistasis focus on tractable systems where it is possible to connect the effects of mutations to the underlying biophysical and molecular mechanisms of the molecular machinery (Dean and Thornton, 2007; Lehner, 2011); namely, RNA sequence-to-shape models (Schuster, 2006), and models of metabolic networks (Szathmáry, 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dean and Thornton, 2007; Lehner, 2011; Schuster, 2006; and Szathmáry, 1993.

claim: RNA sequence-to-shape models and metabolic network models have provided accurate predictions of interactions between mutations.
source: Even though these studies have provided accurate predictions of interactions between mutations, applying their findings to address broader evolutionary questions remains challenging.
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from the text discussing these models.

claim: For RNA sequence-to-shape models, the function of a novel phenotype is impossible to determine without experiments.
source: For RNA sequence-to-shape models, the function of a novel phenotype (new folding structure) is impossible to determine without experiments.
evidence: The claim is stated as a limitation of RNA sequence-to-shape models.

claim: RNA sequence-to-shape models cannot account for the dependence of epistatic interactions on simple variations in cellular environments.
source: In addition, this approach cannot account for the dependence of epistatic interactions on even simple variations in cellular environments, which are known to affect epistasis (Flynn et al., 2013; Caudle et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Flynn et al., 2013 and Caudle et al., 2014.

claim: Metabolic network models are limited to examining the effects of large effect mutations, like deletions and knockouts.
source: On the other hand, metabolic network models are limited to examining the effects of large effect mutations, like deletions and knockouts, and lack an explicit reference to genotype.
evidence: The claim is stated as a limitation of metabolic network models.

claim: Metabolic network models lack an explicit reference to genotype.
source: metabolic network models are limited to examining the effects of large effect mutations, like deletions and knockouts, and lack an explicit reference to genotype.
evidence: The claim is stated as a limitation of metabolic network models.

claim: The molecular biology and biophysics of bacterial gene regulation components are well understood.
source: In order to overcome the limitations of existing theoretical approaches to predicting epistasis, we focused on bacterial regulation of gene expression as one of the simplest model systems in which the molecular biology and biophysics of the interacting components are well understood.
evidence: The claim is stated as a rationale for the study's focus.

claim: Promoters regulated by competitive exclusion of RNAP by a repressor are good candidates for developing a systematic approach to understanding epistasis.
source: Promoters that are regulated by competitive exclusion of RNAP by a repressor are particularly good candidates for developing a systematic approach to understanding epistasis as, in contrast to coding regions as well as more complex CREs and activatable promoters (Garcia et al., 2012), the phenotypic effects of mutations in binding sites of RNAP and repressor are tractable due to their short length and the well-understood biophysical properties of protein-DNA interactions (Bintu et al., 2005b; Saiz and Vilar, 2008; Vilar, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Garcia et al., 2012; Bintu et al., 2005b; Saiz and Vilar, 2008; and Vilar, 2010.

claim: The phenotypic effects of mutations in binding sites of RNAP and repressor are tractable due to their short length and the well-understood biophysical properties of protein-DNA interactions.
source: the phenotypic effects of mutations in binding sites of RNAP and repressor are tractable due to their short length and the well-understood biophysical properties of protein-DNA interactions (Bintu et al., 2005b; Saiz and Vilar, 2008; Vilar, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bintu et al., 2005b; Saiz and Vilar, 2008; and Vilar, 2010.

claim: Understanding the effects of point mutations in the cis-element on the binding properties of RNAP and TFs allows for the construction of a realistic model of transcription initiation.
source: Understanding the effects of point mutations in the cis-element on the binding properties of RNAP and TFs allows for the construction of a realistic model of transcription initiation (Bintu et al., 2005a; Kinney et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bintu et al., 2005a and Kinney et al., 2010.

claim: The study examined epistasis between point mutations in the canonical lambda bacteriophage CRE.
source: Here we studied epistasis between point mutations in the canonical lambda bacteriophage CRE (Ptashne, 2011) (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ptashne, 2011 and reference to Figure 2.

claim: The study employed a fluorescent reporter protein under the control of the strong lambda promoter PR.
source: We employ a fluorescent reporter protein that is under the control of the strong lambda promoter PR (Figure 2a)
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2a showing the experimental system.

claim: The PR promoter is fully repressed by an inducible TF, CI.
source: which is fully repressed by an inducible TF, CI (Figure 2b).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2b showing the repression mechanism.

claim: RNAP and CI have overlapping binding sites in the lambda bacteriophage CRE.
source: RNAP and CI have overlapping binding sites in this CRE, and hence compete for binding.
evidence: The claim is stated as a property of the experimental system.

claim: A library of 141 random double mutants in the CRE was created, with all their corresponding single mutants.
source: We created a library of 141 random double mutants in the CRE, with all their corresponding single mutants (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Supplementary file 1 containing the mutant library data.

claim: The experimental design allows calculation of epistasis in two environments: in the absence of CI and in the presence of CI.
source: This design allows us to calculate epistasis between the mutations in the cis-regulatory element in two environments: in the absence of CI, when only RNAP determines expression; and in the presence of CI when the two proteins compete for binding.
evidence: The claim is stated as a feature of the experimental design.

claim: The majority of double mutants are in negative epistasis in the absence of CI.
source: We observe that the majority of double mutants are in negative epistasis (Figure 3a) — the observed double mutant expression level is lower than the multiplicative expectation based on single mutant expression levels (Pearson's χ21,112=43.82, p<0.0001).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (chi-squared test) and reference to Figure 3a.

claim: 83% of 113 mutants that display statistically significant epistasis exhibit negative epistasis in the absence of CI.
source: Specifically, we observe negative epistasis in 83% of 113 mutants that display statistically significant epistasis, while 28 double mutants do not display significant epistasis (Figure 3a, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 3a and source data.

claim: 28 double mutants do not display significant epistasis in the absence of CI.
source: we observe negative epistasis in 83% of 113 mutants that display statistically significant epistasis, while 28 double mutants do not display significant epistasis (Figure 3a, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 3a and source data.

claim: In a repressible promoter, a reduction in RNAP binding leads to a decrease in gene expression.
source: In a repressible promoter, the effects of mutations on the binding of the two proteins have opposite effects on gene expression — a reduction in RNAP binding leads to a decrease in gene expression
evidence: The claim is stated as a property of repressible promoters.

claim: In a repressible promoter, a reduction in CI binding leads to higher expression levels.
source: a reduction in RNAP binding leads to a decrease in gene expression, while a reduction in CI binding leads to higher expression levels.
evidence: The claim is stated as a property of repressible promoters.

claim: The 141 tested random double mutants show a strong dependence of epistasis on the environment.
source: By comparing epistasis between two environments – absence of CI and high CI concentration – we find that the 141 tested random double mutants show a strong dependence on the environment (ANOVA testing for a GxGxE interaction: F1,280 = 21.77; p<0.0001)
evidence: The claim is supported by ANOVA statistical test showing significant GxGxE interaction.

claim: The environmental dependence of epistasis is in line with previous observations in another bacterial regulatory system.
source: we find that the 141 tested random double mutants show a strong dependence on the environment (ANOVA testing for a GxGxE interaction: F1,280 = 21.77; p<0.0001), in line with previous observations in another bacterial regulatory system (Lagator et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lagator et al., 2016.

claim: 58% of double mutants display a change in the sign of epistasis between the two environments.
source: Interestingly, 58% of double mutants display a change in the sign of epistasis between the two environments (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4.

claim: A switch from negative epistasis in the absence of CI to positive epistasis in its presence is especially prevalent.
source: Especially prevalent is a switch from negative epistasis in the absence of CI, to positive epistasis in its presence (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4.

claim: The proportion of double mutants exhibiting reciprocal sign epistasis is greater in the presence (66%) than in the absence (8%) of CI.
source: Strikingly, the proportion of double mutants exhibiting reciprocal sign epistasis (when the sign of the effect of each mutation changes in the presence of the other mutation) is greater in the presence (66%) than in the absence (8%) of CI (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Supplementary file 2.

claim: The difference in reciprocal sign epistasis likely arises from the molecular architecture of a repressible strong promoter.
source: This difference likely arises from the molecular architecture of a repressible strong promoter.
evidence: The claim is stated as an interpretation of the observed data.

claim: Mutations affect the binding of both DNA-binding proteins.
source: Mutations affect the binding of both DNA-binding proteins, but in the presence of CI the effect on the binding of RNAP is only unmasked when CI does not fully bind
evidence: The claim is stated as an explanation for the observed patterns.

claim: The thermodynamic model is based on statistical thermodynamical assumptions to model the initiation of transcription.
source: In order to understand these observations, we created a model of gene regulation that relies on statistical thermodynamical assumptions to model the initiation of transcription, originally developed to describe gene regulation by the lambda bacteriophage repressor CI (Ackers et al., 1982).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ackers et al., 1982.

claim: The thermodynamic model is generic and does not consider the details of any specific transcription factors involved in regulation.
source: Importantly, our model is generic, as it does not consider the details of any specific transcription factors involved in regulation.
evidence: The claim is stated as a property of the model.

claim: The generic model considers competitive binding between two generic transcription factors that share a single binding site.
source: Instead, we model competitive binding between two generic transcription factors that share a single binding site (Figure 5a).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 5a showing the model structure.

claim: In the thermodynamic model, each DNA-binding protein is assigned a binding energy to an arbitrary stretch of DNA.
source: In the thermodynamic model of transcription, each DNA-binding protein is assigned a binding energy (Ei) to an arbitrary stretch of DNA.
evidence: The claim is stated as a feature of the thermodynamic model.

claim: The model assumes that each position along the single DNA-binding site contributes additively to the global free binding energy.
source: In our formulation, we assume that each position along the single DNA-binding site under consideration contributes additively to the global free binding energy – an assumption found to be accurate at least for a few mutations away from a reference sequence (Vilar, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Vilar, 2010.

claim: Energy contributions can be determined experimentally and are typically represented in the form of an energy matrix.
source: These energy contributions can be determined experimentally (Kinney et al., 2010) and are typically represented in the form of an energy matrix.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kinney et al., 2010.

claim: A Boltzmann weight can be assigned to any configuration of proteins on the promoter.
source: Given a set of DNA-binding proteins (specifically, their energy matrices) and a promoter sequence, a Boltzmann weight can be assigned to any configuration of these proteins on the promoter.
evidence: The claim is stated as a property of the thermodynamic model.

claim: The Boltzmann weight is proportional to the probability of finding the system in each of the possible configurations.
source: The Boltzmann weight is proportional to the probability of finding the system in each of the possible configurations.
evidence: The claim is stated as a property of the thermodynamic model.

claim: The generic model does not make any assumptions about the identity of the TFs that are binding DNA.
source: Note that the model does not make any assumptions about the identity of the TFs that are binding DNA and hence does not utilize any specific energy matrix.
evidence: The claim is stated as a property of the generic model.

claim: The generic model is general in nature, relying only on the physical and mechanistic properties of protein-DNA binding.
source: The model is, therefore, general in nature, relying only on the physical and mechanistic properties of protein-DNA binding.
evidence: The claim is stated as a property of the generic model.

claim: In the generic model, three basic configurations are possible: no proteins bound to DNA, only 'RNAP' bound, or only 'repressor' bound.
source: In our generic model, we consider only a single binding site to which 'repressor' and 'RNAP' compete for binding. Note that the model does not make any assumptions about the identity of the TFs that are binding DNA and hence does not utilize any specific energy matrix. The model is, therefore, general in nature, relying only on the physical and mechanistic properties of protein-DNA binding. In such a system, three basic configurations are possible: no proteins bound to DNA, only 'RNAP' bound, or only 'repressor' bound (Figure 5a).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 5a showing the three configurations.

claim: The generic model does not consider secondary effects of mutations such as effects on DNA structure.
source: As the model does not account for the details of any specific regulatory system, it considers only the direct, primary effects of a mutation on binding affinity (Bintu et al., 2005a), and does not consider any potential interactions arising from secondary effects, namely the effects of a mutation on the structure of DNA (Rajkumar et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bintu et al., 2005a and Rajkumar et al., 2013.

claim: The generic model does not consider effects of mutations on accessibility to the binding sites.
source: does not consider any potential interactions arising from secondary effects, namely the effects of a mutation on the structure of DNA (Rajkumar et al., 2013), accessibility to the binding sites (Levo and Segal, 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Levo and Segal, 2014.

claim: The generic model does not consider effects of mutations on protein cooperativity.
source: accessibility to the binding sites (Levo and Segal, 2014), protein cooperativity (Todeschini et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Todeschini et al., 2014.

claim: The generic model does not consider effects of mutations on looping.
source: protein cooperativity (Todeschini et al., 2014), looping (Levine et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Levine et al., 2014.

claim: The generic model predicts that if mutations have the same sign, they are always in negative epistasis in the absence of repressor.
source: Using the generic model, we first studied the effects of mutations only on 'RNAP' binding (in the absence of 'repressor'), and found that epistasis depends only on the sign of individual mutation effects (Figure 5). Our model predicts that if mutations have the same sign, they are always in negative epistasis.
evidence: The claim is supported by model predictions shown in Figure 5.

claim: When two mutations have a different sign, they will always be in positive epistasis in the absence of repressor.
source: Conversely, when the two mutations have a different sign, they will always be in positive epistasis.
evidence: The claim is stated as a model prediction.

claim: The sign of epistasis for any given TF depends only on the sign of individual mutation effects upon binding.
source: In general, the physical properties of the relationship between binding and gene expression indicate that the sign of epistasis for any given TF depends only on the sign of individual mutation effects (p1 and p2) upon binding (Figure 5c).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 5c showing the general principle.

claim: Experimental observations do not significantly differ from model predictions for the sign of epistasis in the absence of CI.
source: Experimental observations do not significantly differ from these predictions for the sign of epistasis (χ21,112=3.64, p=0.056)
evidence: The claim is supported by chi-squared test showing no significant difference.

claim: 96 of the 113 double mutants (85%) that are in significant epistasis in the absence of CI conform to model predictions.
source: as 96 of the 113 double mutants (85%) that are in significant epistasis in the absence of CI conform to model predictions.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Experimental deviations from the generic model predictions could be due to secondary effects of mutations.
source: Experimental deviations from the generic model predictions (i.e. displaying positive epistasis when both mutations have the same sign) could be due to the secondary effects of mutations, as they could affect the general context of RNAP binding (Rajkumar et al., 2013), or the ability of CI to bind cooperatively (Stayrook et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rajkumar et al., 2013 and Stayrook et al., 2008.

claim: At high 'repressor' concentrations, effects of mutations on 'repressor' binding dominate over their effects on 'RNAP binding'.
source: At high 'repressor' concentrations, effects of mutations on 'repressor' binding dominate over their effects on 'RNAP binding'.
evidence: The claim is stated as a model prediction.

claim: At high repressor concentrations, the sign of epistasis depends only on the sign of individual mutation effects on 'repressor' binding.
source: In these environments, the sign of epistasis depends only on the sign of individual mutation effects on 'repressor' binding.
evidence: The claim is stated as a model prediction.

claim: When one point mutation negatively affects only 'RNAP' binding while the other only 'repressor' binding, the system does not exhibit any epistasis when 'repressor' concentration is very low.
source: When one point mutation negatively affects only 'RNAP' binding, while the other only 'repressor' binding (Figure 5d), the system does not exhibit any epistasis when 'repressor' concentration is very low, as only one of the mutations affects 'RNAP' binding (Figure 5e).
evidence: The claim is supported by model predictions shown in Figures 5d and 5e.

claim: As 'repressor' concentration increases, the system is in positive epistasis when one mutation affects only RNAP and the other only repressor.
source: As 'repressor' concentration increases, the system is in positive epistasis.
evidence: The claim is stated as a model prediction.

claim: At very high 'repressor' concentrations, epistasis approaches 0 as the 'repressor' binds too strongly.
source: Finally, at very high 'repressor' concentrations, which are probably not biologically relevant, epistasis approaches 0 as the 'repressor' binds too strongly.
evidence: The claim is stated as a model prediction.

claim: When point mutations negatively affect both 'RNAP' and 'repressor' binding, epistasis changes the sign from negative to positive as 'repressor' concentration increases.
source: When point mutations negatively affect both 'RNAP' and 'repressor' binding (Figure 5f), epistasis changes the sign from negative to positive as 'repressor' concentration increases (Figure 5g).
evidence: The claim is supported by model predictions shown in Figures 5f and 5g.

claim: The generic model explains the observation that most double mutants change the sign of epistasis between the two environments.
source: As most experimentally tested mutations reduce both RNAP and CI binding, our model explains the observation that most double mutants change the sign of epistasis between the two environments (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by model predictions and reference to Figure 4.

claim: Energy matrices for RNAP and CI were used to create five random double mutants for each possible combination of single mutation effects.
source: To obtain this information, we used the experimentally determined energy matrices for RNAP (Kinney et al., 2010) and CI (Sarai and Takeda, 1989), and utilized it to create five random double mutants for each possible combination of single mutation effects shown in Table 1.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kinney et al., 2010 and Sarai and Takeda, 1989.

claim: Point mutations that simultaneously improved the binding of both RNAP and CI could not be identified due to the high specificity of binding.
source: Due to the high specificity of binding of both RNAP and CI, we could not identify point mutations that simultaneously improved the binding of both (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Supplementary file 3.

claim: The model was validated by measuring epistasis in 30 double mutants in the two environments.
source: Therefore, we validate the model by measuring epistasis in 30 double mutants (five for each of the six possible combinations of single mutant effects) in the two environments.
evidence: The claim is stated as part of the experimental validation.

claim: There is no difference between the predicted and experimental estimates of the sign of epistasis and its dependence on the two experimental environments.
source: We find no difference between the predicted and experimental estimates of the sign of epistasis and its dependence on the two experimental environments (Pearson's χ22,30=0.68; p=0.72) (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by chi-squared test and reference to Figure 6.

claim: The predictions about the sign of epistasis that arise from the generic model hold true in the experimental system.
source: As such, the predictions about the sign of epistasis that arise from the generic model (Table 1) hold true in our experimental system.
evidence: The claim is supported by the validation experiment results.

claim: The thermodynamic model predicts not only the sign but also the magnitude of epistasis in the absence of CI.
source: When we excluded those double mutants which did not empirically exhibit significant epistasis, we found a significant fit between experimental measurements and model predictions of the magnitude of epistasis in the absence (F1,15 = 9.86; p<0.01)
evidence: The claim is supported by linear regression analysis showing significant fit.

claim: The thermodynamic model predicts not only the sign but also the magnitude of epistasis in the presence of CI.
source: we found a significant fit between experimental measurements and model predictions of the magnitude of epistasis in the absence (F1,15 = 9.86; p<0.01) and in the presence of CI (F1,15 = 4.59; p<0.05) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by linear regression analysis and reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The model predicts the magnitude of epistasis without considering detailed molecular aspects of the experimental system such as CI dimerization or cooperativity.
source: As such, the model predicts not only the general patterns of epistasis (sign), but is also reasonably accurate at predicting its magnitude, which is remarkable since the model does not consider detailed molecular aspects of the experimental system, such as CI dimerization or cooperativity.
evidence: The claim is stated as an interpretation of the model's predictive power.

claim: The theory provides an accurate prediction of the sign of epistasis and its environmental dependence for a repressible promoter system.
source: The theory we present here, which is based on mechanistic properties of protein-DNA binding without accounting for any details of the molecular system studied, provides an accurate prediction of the sign of epistasis and its environmental dependence for a repressible promoter system
evidence: The claim is stated as a summary of the study's findings.

claim: Repressible promoter systems are the most common form of gene regulation in E. coli (~40% of all regulated genes).
source: provides an accurate prediction of the sign of epistasis and its environmental dependence for a repressible promoter system - the most common form of gene regulation in E. coli (~40% of all regulated genes [Salgado et al., 2013]).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Salgado et al., 2013.

claim: The results are derived from first principles because the generic model has no reference to any particular empirical measures.
source: Furthermore, the fact that we use a generic model with no reference to any particular empirical measures means that our results are derived from first principles.
evidence: The claim is stated as a property of the approach.

claim: The results should hold as long as the effects of mutations on gene expression are mainly driven by their direct impact on TF-DNA binding.
source: As such, the presented results should hold as long as the effects of mutations on gene expression are mainly driven by their direct impact on TF-DNA binding, as represented by the energy matrix for a given TF.
evidence: The claim is stated as a condition for the applicability of the results.

claim: The thermodynamic model, rather than the multiplicative (or additive) expectation, provides a meaningful null model for the sign of epistasis in CREs.
source: Under such conditions, the thermodynamic model, rather than the multiplicative (or additive) expectation, provides a meaningful null model for the sign of epistasis in CREs.
evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion of the study.

claim: The sign of the deviations from a multiplicative expectation can have important evolutionary consequences for the evolution of sex.
source: The sign of the deviations from a multiplicative expectation can have important evolutionary consequences, such as for the evolution of sex (Otto and Lenormand, 2002)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Otto and Lenormand, 2002.

claim: The sign of the deviations from a multiplicative expectation can have important evolutionary consequences for the maintenance of genetic variation.
source: The sign of the deviations from a multiplicative expectation can have important evolutionary consequences, such as for the evolution of sex (Otto and Lenormand, 2002) or the maintenance of genetic variation (Charlesworth et al., 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Charlesworth et al., 1995.

claim: Sign epistasis can lead to the existence of multiple optima (local peaks).
source: A particularly important pattern of epistasis is sign epistasis, where the sign of the effect of a particular substitution depends on the genetic background. Sign epistasis can lead to the existence of multiple optima (local peaks).
evidence: The claim is stated as a property of sign epistasis.

claim: In the system analyzed, sign epistasis cannot exist in the absence of a repressor.
source: In the system we analyze here, sign epistasis cannot exist in the absence of a repressor, since there is an optimum binding site sequence and the effects of mutations have a definite sign toward this optimal sequence.
evidence: The claim is stated as a property of the system.

claim: In the presence of a repressor, sign epistasis is possible.
source: In the presence of a repressor, however, sign epistasis is possible (Poelwijk et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Poelwijk et al., 2011.

claim: The sign of epistasis very often reverses between environments.
source: Furthermore, we show that the sign of epistasis very often reverses between environments.
evidence: The claim is stated as a finding of the study.

claim: The environmental reversal of epistasis sign was previously observed in a different system.
